files.notes/close_checklist.md:
# June 2026 close — controller checklist

Prepared by E. Nakamura. Complete in sequence; no shortcuts:

1. Reconcile operating cash to the June bank statement. For every book-side item identified by the reconciliation, propose one correcting journal entry per item.
2. Review the payroll register for any pay period ending after 6/30 that pays in July. If one exists, accrue the full gross wages to Accrued Liabilities; note that in some months every run pays in-month.
3. Confirm June prepaid amortization against the prepaid schedule and supporting contracts. Check the GL first to avoid a duplicate. If the entry is missing, book June prepaid amortization as ONE combined journal entry. Apply the convention that a full month is taken in the month an item begins.
4. Book June depreciation per the fixed asset register, after verifying the amount has not already been posted to the GL.
5. Compare the June vendor-bill documents with the GL coding. Verify that each expense is in the correct account and reclass anything miscoded.
6. Prepare June budget-vs-actual variance commentary on an as-closed basis, after items 1-5 have been booked.
files.notes/company_background.md:
# Company background

Fathom Analytics Co. began when a small group of product-minded analysts grew tired of watching operating teams wait days for answers that were already buried in their systems. They built a lightweight internal dashboard that pulled scattered business data into a shared, readable view. Colleagues kept asking for access, and the tool gradually became a company.

Today, Fathom Analytics Co. sells hosted analytics software for growing organizations that need practical reporting without a large data department. The platform connects common business systems, organizes recurring metrics, and gives customers configurable dashboards, scheduled reporting, and tools for investigating changes. Its customers tend to be finance, operations, and customer teams that want dependable answers without maintaining a complicated reporting stack.

The team has the flavor of a compact SaaS shop: engineers sit close to support, product conversations include real customer examples, and salespeople are expected to understand the software rather than simply deliver a pitch. Internal communication is direct, occasionally dry, and heavy on shared notes.

The company remains an ordinary going concern. Its current focus is improving onboarding, sharpening its market position, and making internal processes more repeatable as the customer base develops. Leadership is also tightening month-end routines so operating decisions rest on timely, well-supported information.
files.notes/marketing_plan_h2.md:
# H2 marketing plan — working draft

## What we are trying to accomplish

Give Fathom Analytics Co. a clearer, more consistent market presence without sanding off the practical voice customers already recognize. The brand refresh should emphasize useful answers, approachable reporting, and fast adoption by operating teams.

## Core programs

- Complete the brand refresh across the website, sales materials, product screenshots, and customer-facing templates.
- Host two educational webinars per quarter. Keep the sessions tactical: reporting hygiene, metric ownership, and better operating reviews.
- Develop a partner co-marketing pilot with a complementary software or advisory firm. Start narrowly, agree on audience and ownership, then document what is repeatable.
- Turn strong customer questions into short articles, product demonstrations, and sales enablement notes.
- Build a lightweight customer-story pipeline with support and account conversations as the primary source.

## Working approach

Use Q2 close findings to finalize the available budget and sequence the work. Favor reusable content over isolated campaigns, and avoid launching more channels than the team can maintain well.

## Measures to watch

Track qualified interest, webinar engagement, partner-sourced conversations, content reuse by sales, and whether refreshed messaging improves the quality of discovery calls. Review results at each quarter-end and adjust the mix rather than adding activity for its own sake.

# Handoff from your chatty predecessor

For E. Nakamura — a few things that are easy to miss if nobody tells you:

- The bank tends to slip its own service fees and charges onto the last statement days. We have historically booked those at close rather than during the month, so check near the end of the statement.
- June got busy, and some vendor-bill expense coding may be off. Please compare the GL with the underlying documents; the files in bills/ are authoritative.
- The Q2 budget was fixed in early April. The one-off items that landed in June were therefore never planned, and they are the main reason the variances look large.
- Payroll timing is unusual this time: the second June run pays in early July. Check the register before posting the accrual.
